column4: The section's city is a bounded place of gathering and safety; this ayah calls the House a place of return for people and a place of security, making the sanctuary a shared civic center.

The section cites Abraham's request for this balad to be safe and provisioned; this ayah joins safety and fruit to a limit on the disbeliever's enjoyment and a final fire, showing the city's abundance as a tested gift.
The section's dictionary forms B004-B005 pair al-hady with its maḥill; this ayah makes shaving wait until the offering reaches its place, so arrival at that place governs the rite.
The section's Meccan balad is named here as Bakkah: the first House for humanity, blessed and guidance for all, locating the sanctuary within a wider human gathering.
The section presents the city as a place of protection; this ayah says whoever enters the House is safe and makes pilgrimage there a duty, joining safety to arrival.

The section defines dictionary form qurbān as an offering brought near to God; the sons of Adam each present a قُرْبَانًا, and the ayah distinguishes the offering accepted by God from the one rejected.

The section's hady is an offering carried to its place; this ayah requires a replacement offering هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ for a hunting violation in the sacred state, tying sanctuary boundaries to sacrifice.
The section makes the city a scene of safety and provision; this ayah says God made the Kaaba a support for people, alongside the sacred month and offerings, so the House sustains communal life.

The section's dictionary form hadī (B007) is a person who comes to a group seeking protection; here a polytheist who asks for protection is granted it and escorted to a safe place, making refuge a concrete duty.

The section names a truce between enemies and Muslims and a person with or without an ahd; this ayah specifies a covenant made at the Sacred Mosque and commands reciprocal fidelity while the other party keeps it.
The section's balad is a settled city whose residents give it its character; Abraham asks that this very balad be made safe, grounding the civic image in a prayer for protection.

The section says a city's ability to house people depends on provision; Abraham says he settled some descendants in a barren valley by the sacred House and asks for hearts to incline and fruit to reach them.

The section's dictionary sense B004 of ح ل ل is that punishment descends; this ayah warns that God's anger may come down on those who transgress and says the one it reaches has fallen, turning a settled community's security into exposure.

The section defines the city through those who reside there; this ayah makes residents and visitors from afar equal at the Sacred Mosque, while condemning those who bar access, showing how a sacred place gathers people and sets a boundary.

The section describes place as bounded and shaped by its inhabitants; this ayah says God established the place of the House for Abraham and commands its purification, grounding the boundary in a deliberate act.
The section joins hady, provision and the miskin; this ayah has pilgrims mention God over livestock He provided and feed the distressed poor, linking offerings to sustenance for the vulnerable.
The section's dictionary form maḥill is the destination of hady; this ayah says the animals' final place is the Ancient House, directly placing the offering at its destination.
The section links a city to provision for the miskin; this ayah makes sacrificial camels a sign and commands people to eat from them and feed both the needy and the one who asks.
The section's city is sacred and inhabited; the speaker says he was commanded to worship the Lord of this town, the One who made it sacred, joining the city's boundary to worship.
The section places security and fruit in one city; people fear that following guidance will get them snatched from their land, and the reply points to a secure sanctuary to which fruit is brought.
The section makes the city a protected place; this ayah asks whether people see that a secure sanctuary stands amid surrounding abduction, so its safety is a real boundary against danger.

The section calls the city a place marked by its inhabitants and their staying; this ayah locates Saba's sign in their dwelling, with gardens, provision and a good town, showing settlement as nourished life.

The section's dictionary sense B002 of ح ل ل is settling in a place; this ayah says God settled the believers in the abode of permanence by His bounty, giving that verb family a lasting, secure destination.

The section places protection and lack of protection inside the city; this ayah says God restrained both sides' hands in the middle of Mecca, while 48:25 adds that the offering was held back from its place, showing restraint within the sanctuary conflict.

The section connects the sanctuary, the offering's destination and release from ihram; this ayah promises entry into the Sacred Mosque safely, without fear, with heads shaved or shortened, reversing the blocked access of 48:25.
The section cites this city as a place of safety; the oath names وَهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ, giving the city itself the quality Abraham prayed for elsewhere.
The section makes the populated city a place of shelter and provision; this ayah tells Quraysh to worship the Lord of this House, tying the community's life to its sanctuary.
The section says that a city's ability to shelter people rests on provision; this ayah says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear, joining sustenance and safety.

The section's dictionary sense B004 of ح ل ل is that punishment descends; this ayah says a calamity may come near the disbelievers' homes, bringing that root's downward arrival into the city-and-dwelling scene.

The section names q-r-b both in the orphan's kinship and in dictionary form qurbān; this ayah joins close relatives, orphans and the needy as recipients of wealth, showing social nearness beside an offering's nearness to God.

The section explores the boundary between the sacred state and release from it; this ayah tests believers with game within reach while they are in that state, giving the boundary a concrete restraint on taking.

The section notes that ح ل ل can name release from a sacred limit; this ayah contrasts permitted sea game and food for travelers with forbidden land game while in ihram, making the boundary govern provision.

The section's root note B008 gives q-s-m the dictionary sense of a truce between enemies; this ayah says that if the enemy inclines to peace, the believers should incline to it, stating the truce's reciprocal action.
The section names an ahd as what protects a person; this ayah commands that treaties with polytheists who kept them be completed to their term, clarifying how protection lasts by a kept covenant.
The section makes a city an arrival point where a person may be safe; Joseph tells his family to enter Egypt safely, a separate scene of secure entry into a settled land.

The section's dictionary sense B004 is punishment coming down; this adjacent ayah adds that earlier messengers were mocked and the deniers were eventually seized, completing 13:31's warning of calamity near their homes.
The section says a city gathers those who settle and arrive; this ayah calls people to pilgrimage and depicts them arriving on foot and by camel from distant passes.
The section places the offering at the Ancient House; after the pilgrimage rites in 22:28, this ayah adds fulfilling vows and circumambulating the House, showing what arrival at that place completes.
The section cites the lasting abode in 35:35; the preceding ayah says its people praise God for removing grief, completing the secure-home image with release from sorrow.

The section gathers safety, hostility and truce in the Meccan sanctuary; this ayah contrasts the disbelievers' zeal with God's sending calm upon the Messenger and believers, continuing the restrained confrontation of 48:24-25.

The section's dictionary form hadī describes someone seeking shelter with a group; this ayah describes poor emigrants driven from their homes and possessions, making the need for a receiving community concrete.

The section's hadī is one who comes to a people for protection; this ayah describes the residents who made the abode and faith their own and loved those who migrated to them, showing shelter as a communal welcome.

The section's root note for miskin links it to dwelling and says provision makes dwelling possible; this ayah names the needy alongside the orphan and captive as people given food, showing the sustenance at stake in that dwelling.

The section says city life depends on provision; this ayah names Quraysh's winter and summer journeys, while 106:3-4 connect the community to the House, food and security, showing movement behind the city's provision.
The section defines qurbān as what is brought near to God; this ayah calls spending قُرُبَاتٍ عِندَ اللَّهِ, explicitly treating material giving as a means of nearness.
The section treats the city's sacred boundary and a truce as limits on exposure; this ayah forbids transgression in fighting, and 2:191 applies the limit specifically at the Sacred Mosque.

The section says the same word-family can place a person outside the sanctuary's protection; this ayah forbids fighting at the Sacred Mosque unless the other side fights there, defining the boundary of its safety.
The section develops a truce between enemies; following 2:191's conditional fighting at the Sacred Mosque, this ayah says that if the other side stops, God is forgiving and merciful.

The section's truce sense of q-s-m meets this limit on conflict: after the call to fight until persecution ends, this ayah says there is no aggression if the other side stops, except against wrongdoers.
The section treats a sanctuary as a protected boundary; this ayah says sacred months and things have reciprocal limits and answers transgression only in equal measure.
The section makes the city a possible place of shelter; the oppressed here ask to be brought out of a town whose people are wrongdoers and for a protecting ally, showing the reverse of a safe abode.

The section's root ح ل ل has two stated faces: violating sacred things and leaving ihram; this ayah forbids violating the sacred signs and hady, then permits hunting once people have left the sacred state.

The section's sanctuary is a place of protection; this ayah says disbelievers bar people from the Sacred Mosque and denies that they are its guardians, reversing the idea that mere presence confers its protection.

The section says residents shape the city they inhabit; this adjacent ayah describes the disbelievers' conduct at the House as whistling and clapping and links it to punishment, showing a sanctuary dishonored by its occupants.

The section joins a sacred city's boundary to its provision; this ayah bars polytheists from the Sacred Mosque, then answers fear of poverty with God's promise of enrichment, setting exclusion beside provision.
The section's dictionary sense B002 of ح ل ل is settling in an abode; this ayah says wrongdoers settled their people in the house of ruin, reversing the secure dwelling.

The section contrasts settling in a permanent home with destructive settlement; following 14:28's house of ruin, this ayah identifies that destination as Hell, showing the consequence of the placement.
The section pictures the city as sheltered and well-provisioned; this ayah's town is initially secure and supplied from every place, then disbelief turns that condition into hunger and fear.

The section defines qurbān as what is brought near to God and traces hady to its physical place; this ayah says meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does, distinguishing arrival at the House from spiritual acceptance.

The section defines a town through its settled residents and its provision; this ayah says many towns grew insolent in their livelihood and their homes remained nearly uninhabited after them, reversing the nourished dwelling.

The section calls a city a place shaped by the life of its residents; this ayah says Saba turned away and a flood replaced their two gardens with bitter growth, turning a provision-rich dwelling into loss.
The section sets a fed city beside its residents' conduct; following Saba's lost gardens in 34:16, this ayah names disbelief as the recompense, completing the reversal of provision.
The section says a city's residents shape its condition; this ayah says towns would have received blessings from heaven and earth had their people believed, but denial brought seizure.
The section makes the city a scene of safety; this ayah asks whether town-dwellers felt secure from God's punishment arriving by night while they slept.
The section makes a city a sheltering place; this adjacent ayah asks whether its people felt secure from punishment arriving by day while they played.
The section holds urban security beside the possibility of punishment; this ayah closes the questions in 7:97-98 by asking whether the town-dwellers felt safe from God's plan.
The section links the miskin's ability to dwell to provision; this ayah condemns the one who will not urge feeding الْمِسْكِينِ, showing the social failure that leaves the needy without sustenance.
